Server health.title: A health check with a memory
Server health.summary: Take 1 built a probe for disk, memory and web availability, then taught it to keep the last 32 checks. It added certificate expiry and request timings. The latest timing change breaks local requests into the connection, header and body phases so there's more evidence when a request is slow.

Radio Survey.title: Find the hidden radio transmitter
Radio Survey.summary: Four receivers give distance ranges to a transmitter hidden on a grid. Take 1 checked 730 daily puzzles and found exactly one solution per puzzle, with all four clues needed. It added overlays so players can see which squares fit a clue.

Sandpile simulation.title: How many grains before the first spill?
Sandpile simulation.summary: Take 1 simulated dropping grains at the center of a grid. On a 31×31 board, the 1,768th grain sent 36 over the edge. It also showed that the final pattern survives changes in processing order and fits into a 35-byte wedge when stored by symmetry.

Sandpile chime.title: What a sandpile sounds like
Sandpile chime.summary: Take 1 turned the same first-spill simulation into a 4.45-second chime. Busier rounds rise in pitch, and rounds that spill grains over the edge get a separate high tone.

Sandpile animation.title: Watch the first spill spread
Sandpile animation.summary: An eight-second animation follows the 1,768th grain through 99 rounds of toppling. The first four grains escape in round 36, and 36 escape in total.

Error correction.title: Repairing a burst of flipped bits
Error correction.summary: Take 1's decoder repaired every single-bit error and flagged every two-bit error in its test. It then interleaved the bits across four bytes, which let the same decoder recover from all 29 placements of a four-bit burst.

Orbit Lab.title: Two ways to simulate an orbit
Orbit Lab.summary: Take 1 ran two simulations of the same elliptical orbit. Forward Euler spiraled outward and hit 85.5% peak energy error. Velocity Verlet stayed near the ellipse at 0.74%, and doubling the number of steps cut its angular lag from 14.8° to 3.74°.
Orbit Lab.imageAlt: The Euler orbit spirals out while the Verlet orbit stays close to the reference ellipse.

Random walks.title: Does a random walker ever get home?
Random walks.summary: Take 1 calculated the chance of returning to the starting point at least once within 4,000 steps. It found 98.7% on a line, 71.8% on a square grid, and 33.6% on a cubic grid.

Bit patterns and position decoding.title: A ruler made of bits
Bit patterns and position decoding.summary: Take 1 made a 32-bit loop where five clean bits identify your position. It searched all 2,048 candidate loops and found designs that need only ten bits to tolerate one wrong reading. Its decoder can also handle a wrong bit and an unreadable one together with fourteen bits.

Chaos and rounding.title: How long does extra precision buy you?
Chaos and rounding.summary: In Take 1's logistic-map experiment, starting a million times closer bought a median of just 20 more steps before the trajectories separated. It later showed that changing how a low-precision calculation rounds can send the same system into completely different repeating loops.

VPS Lab gallery.title: A searchable offline gallery for the experiments
VPS Lab gallery.summary: Take 1 added search by title and filename and brought 17 recent experiments and tools into its offline gallery. It ran all 53 listed commands from a fresh extraction and rebuilt the 85-file ZIP byte for byte.

Leap-day calendar.title: A calendar you can listen to
Leap-day calendar.summary: Assuming a fixed year length of 365.24219 days, Take 1 found that 31 leap days per 128 years was the closest fit among cycles up to 400 years. It turned the schedule into a ten-second rhythm, with a louder click for each leap year.

Musical tuning.title: Why two nearly identical chords pulse differently
Musical tuning.summary: Take 1 made clips comparing pure tuning with evenly spaced notes. The major third pulsed 8.73 times per second with the usual 12 divisions of an octave. Using 53 divisions brought the beat down to about 0.89 per second.

Sharding and load balancing.title: Adding a server without moving everything
Sharding and load balancing.summary: In a test with 20,000 keys, adding a ninth shard moved 88.67% of keys with ordinary modulo hashing and 10.76% with rendezvous hashing. In a separate test, assigning each key to the less busy of two candidates cut the peak load.

Spatial indexing.title: Reading a rectangle from a one-dimensional file
Spatial indexing.summary: Take 1 stored the same grid in row, Morton and Hilbert order. In its model, reading about eight extra tiles per query cut the Hilbert layout from 7.69 separate reads to 4.30 on average.

Cache replacement.title: When a bigger cache misses more often
Cache replacement.summary: Take 1 found the shortest request sequence in its search where adding a slot hurts a first-in, first-out cache. The 12 requests cause nine misses with three slots and ten with four, and the same counts recur on every repeat.

Sampling π.title: Estimating π by spreading out the guesses
Sampling π.summary: Take 1 estimated π by dropping points inside a square and counting how many landed in a circle. Giving each grid cell one sample cut the trial-to-trial error by over sixfold. It improved the estimate again by reflecting a second point across each cell's center.

Audio compression.title: Shrinking WAV files without losing samples
Audio compression.summary: Instead of storing every audio sample as-is, Take 1 stored how samples change. Its best versions saved 64.5% of the sandpile sample bytes and roughly 77% of the tuning sample bytes, while reconstructing every sample exactly.

Balance-scale puzzles.title: Four weights, one of them missing
Balance-scale puzzles.summary: Weights of 1, 3, 9 and 27 can balance every integer mass from 1 to 40. Take 1 then asked what coverage survives when any weight goes missing. It found that 1, 2, 4 and 7 guarantee every mass from 1 to 7 and proved that four weights cannot guarantee eight.

Random identifier collisions.title: How many bits does a random ID need?
Random identifier collisions.summary: Take 1 calculated the chance that two randomly chosen identifiers collide. For one million independent, uniformly random IDs and a risk budget of one in a million, 59 bits was the smallest width that met the budget.

Numerically stable roots.title: Recovering the tiny root a calculator loses
Numerically stable roots.summary: Take 1 found an equation where the direct quadratic formula rounds a real root near one billionth to zero. It recovered the small root from the large one and then scaled the calculation to avoid overflow with much larger coefficients.

Queue scheduling.title: What happens to long jobs in a fast queue?
Queue scheduling.summary: Take 1 simulated a server handling both short and long jobs. Always picking the shortest cut the overall wait but made long jobs wait more. Raising the priority of jobs as they waited reduced that penalty.

Proportional allocation.title: A fourth seat that costs someone their first
Proportional allocation.summary: Take 1 found that with weights 3, 3 and 1, largest-remainder allocation gives every group one seat out of three. With four seats, the same groups get 2, 2 and 0. It also found a case where a different method gives a group more than its proportional quota.

Floating-point accuracy.title: What arithmetic forgets near a big number
Floating-point accuracy.summary: Adding large positive numbers, ones and large negative numbers in the wrong order made the ones disappear. Take 1 compared summation methods that preserve them, then recovered the exact variance of 40,000 values near 10¹⁶ from summaries of 315 batches.

Black-and-white dithering.title: One bit of gray
Black-and-white dithering.summary: Take 1 rendered a smooth gray ramp with black and white pixels by varying the density of white dots. Repeating a fixed pattern compressed the image to a few hundred bytes. Randomizing each tile independently produced nearly the same local brightness and a much larger file.

Grid pathfinding.title: A useful hint for a maze with one opening
Grid pathfinding.summary: A distance hint cut a search across an open grid from 2,076 visited cells to 62. On a map with a wall, telling the search where the opening was let it visit just the 184 cells along one shortest route.

Pascal triangle fractals.title: The patterns hiding in Pascal’s triangle
Pascal triangle fractals.summary: Mark only the odd entries and a Sierpiński triangle appears. Take 1 drew the repeating patterns for remainders modulo 2, 3 and 5 and checked each plotted entry against the exact binomial coefficients.
Pascal triangle fractals.imageAlt: Three triangular fractals from Pascal’s triangle with different colors for each nonzero remainder.

Thumbnail sampling.title: A checkerboard that disappears in a thumbnail
Thumbnail sampling.summary: Taking every second pixel made the same checkerboard turn solid black or solid white, depending on where sampling started. Averaging each block kept it gray. A second test showed that rounding after each of two shrinking stages can brighten the result by one level.

Riffle shuffles.title: How random is a deck after seven shuffles?
Riffle shuffles.summary: Take 1 calculated how far ideal riffle shuffles leave a 52-card deck from a perfectly random one. The probability gap fell from 0.614 after six shuffles to 0.334 after seven and below 0.1 after nine.

Coin-flip patterns.title: The slower pattern that wins the race
Coin-flip patterns.summary: Take 1 calculated how long different eight-flip patterns take to appear. It then put two on the same stream of coin flips and found one that waits longer on its own yet wins 66.84% of their head-to-head races.

Audio aliasing.title: A rising tone that seems to fall
Audio aliasing.summary: Take 1 played a three-second sweep from 1 to 7 kHz. In the 8 kHz recording, the pitch rises to 4 kHz and then falls back to 1 kHz because the sampling rate makes higher pitches appear as lower ones.

Shut the Box.title: A better way to play Shut the Box
Shut the Box.summary: Take 1 solved the two-dice game across all 512 board states. Optimal play won 7.14% of games. Always clearing as many tiles as possible won 1.10%, even when ties were broken optimally.

Bloom filters.title: When distinct hash positions make a filter worse
Bloom filters.summary: Take 1 tested a tiny probabilistic membership filter. Requiring distinct positions reduced false positives with three probes. With eight probes it filled too much of the filter, raising false positives from 19.11% to 30.36%.

Polynomial interpolation.title: When more sample points make a curve fit worse
Polynomial interpolation.summary: Going from 5 to 21 evenly spaced points pushed the biggest measured error from 0.44 to 59.82. The same number of points clustered near the ends brought it down from 0.46 to 0.018.
Polynomial interpolation.imageAlt: Interpolation error rises with evenly spaced points and falls with points clustered near the ends.

Daylight saving time.title: The alarm time that goes missing
Daylight saving time.summary: Take 1 checked a daily 1:30 a.m. schedule in London. In 2026, that time occurs zero times on the spring clock-change date and twice in autumn. Counting both autumn occurrences puts those two alarms just an hour apart.

Pixel perimeter.title: Measuring a circle made of square pixels
Pixel perimeter.summary: Counting exposed pixel edges overestimated a circle's circumference by about 27%. Counting diagonal crossings as well brought the error down to 0.015% at a radius of 2,048 pixels, though the same estimator undercounted a square.

Pairs of distance rulers.title: Two different rulers with the same distances
Pairs of distance rulers.summary: Take 1 found two dissimilar arrangements of six marks whose 15 pairwise distances are exactly the same. It searched all shorter spans and found that 17 is the minimum when every distance must be distinct.

Langton’s ant.title: The ant that builds a diagonal highway
Langton’s ant.summary: Take 1 put an ant on a blank grid with two rules. It turns based on a tile's color and flips that color as it leaves. After 9,977 steps, it fell into a 104-step pattern that repeats while moving diagonally.

Shortlist selection.title: How long should you wait before making a shortlist?
Shortlist selection.summary: Take 1 worked through 52 candidates arriving in random order, when you can only rank the people you've already seen. Having two shortlist spots raised the best chance of including the top candidate from 37.40% to 60.10%.

Maze generation.title: A maze generator with a favorite layout
Maze generation.summary: Take 1 shuffled the walls and opened only those that connected separate areas. In a 3×3 maze, some resulting layouts were nearly twice as likely as others. The most common appeared 0.685% of the time, versus 0.351% for the least common.

Empty seats.title: How many seats get stranded when people sit in pairs?
Empty seats.summary: Take 1 assigned pairs of adjacent seats at random until every remaining empty seat was isolated. In a row of 100, about 14 seats were left empty on average. The chance of filling the entire row was about one in 58 million.

Traffic ring.title: How fast can a traffic jam clear on a loop?
Traffic ring.summary: Take 1 put six bumper-to-bumper cars on a 12-space loop and let each car advance when the next space was empty. One car could move at first. After five updates all six could move every time. The script checked all 4,096 starting layouts on that loop.

Dice cycle.title: Three dice that beat one another in a loop
Dice cycle.summary: Take 1 split the numbers 1 through 15 among three five-sided dice with the same average roll. In the strongest sets, A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A. Each matchup favors its winner 60% of the time, even though all three dice average 8.

Probe coverage.title: How easily can a short outage slip between checks?
Probe coverage.summary: Take 1 measured the gaps in 32 saved HTTPS checks. For a uniformly timed outage within the observed window, five minutes of downtime would miss every check about 88% of the time. A 30-minute outage would still go undetected about 42% of the time.

Phase coverage.title: Catching an outage that repeats at the same time
Phase coverage.summary: Take 1 modeled an outage that lasts five minutes and starts at the same minute every hour. A check at a fixed minute caught only about one in twelve possible start times. Shifting the check minute back and forth covered them all within 24 probes.

Random probe gaps.title: The blind spots left by randomly timed checks
Random probe gaps.summary: Take 1 calculated the gaps left by placing 24 checks at independent random minutes and seconds around a repeating hour. The largest gap averaged 9.44 minutes. Only about one schedule in 900 kept every gap to five minutes or less.

Ordered codes.title: What it costs to keep a compressed alphabet in order
Ordered codes.summary: Take 1 compared binary codes for three symbols when the middle symbol was 100 times as frequent as either neighbor. Requiring the codewords to follow symbol order raised the average from 1.02 to 1.99 bits per symbol. Moving the frequent symbol first erased the difference.

Mono fold.title: How mixing to mono can make tones disappear
Mono fold.summary: Take 1 recorded three tones and mixed them with a copy delayed by one millisecond. The 500 Hz and 1,500 Hz tones canceled because the delay put them half a cycle out of phase. The 1,000 Hz tone stayed in phase and survived the mix.

Coin change lab.title: Four coins that make change with fewer pieces
Coin change lab.summary: Take 1 searched 18,424 four-denomination systems for amounts from 1 to 99. The sets 1, 5, 18, 25 and 1, 5, 18, 29 both averaged 3.93 coins with optimal choices. Requiring the largest usable coin at each step raised the best average to 4.14.

Hedge latency.title: When a backup request makes the slowest responses faster
Hedge latency.summary: In Take 1’s model, 5% of requests took 200 ms. Launching a duplicate after 30 ms cut the 99th-percentile time to 50 ms when delays were independent, at the cost of 5% more requests. The benefit disappeared when the two requests were sufficiently likely to slow down together.

Pascal powers.title: Counting odd numbers in a million rows of Pascal’s triangle
Pascal powers.summary: Take 1 used digit carries to count divisibility across the first 1,048,576 rows. Only 0.634% of the roughly 550 billion entries were odd, and 8.359% had a nonzero remainder when divided by 16. It checked the shortcut against direct calculations on smaller triangles.

Fraction rounding.title: How a flexible denominator improves fraction rounding
Fraction rounding.summary: Take 1 rounded numbers between zero and one to fractions. Letting the denominator vary up to 100 reduced the mean error from 0.0025 to 0.000189 compared with using 100 throughout. Both methods still had a worst-case error of 0.005.

Coin extractor.title: Getting fair random bits from a biased coin
Coin extractor.summary: For a coin that lands heads 20% of the time, Take 1 recovered 0.160 fair bits per flip by working in pairs and 0.646 by working in blocks of 64. It exhaustively checked small blocks to make sure outputs of the same length were equally likely.

Queue variability.title: Why a few slow jobs can hold up the whole queue
Queue variability.summary: Take 1 compared two single-worker queues at 80% utilization, each with a 10 ms average job. When jobs ranged from 1 to 91 ms, the mean wait rose from 20 ms to about 166 ms. The delay grows because an arrival can get stuck behind one of the unusually long jobs.

Fourier windows.title: Measuring a tone between two frequency bins
Fourier windows.summary: Take 1 measured a tone that sat halfway between two frequencies in a Fourier analysis. An untapered sample read 3.92 dB low. A Hann window brought that error down to 1.42 dB by tapering the ends, while spreading the peak across more bins.

Grid reliability.title: Where one extra link helps a grid the most
Grid reliability.summary: Take 1 tested eight places to add a diagonal to a 3×3 grid whose links worked independently 90% of the time. Connecting either target corner to the center raised the chance of a working corner-to-corner path from 97.25% to 98.48%.

Chord lab.title: Why a random chord has three different answers
Chord lab.summary: Take 1 asked how often a chord is longer than a side of the equilateral triangle inside the same circle. The probability was one third when choosing random endpoints, one half when choosing a random distance from the center, and one quarter when choosing a random midpoint in the disk.

Huffman ties.title: Same compression, shorter worst-case code
Huffman ties.summary: Take 1 changed how a Huffman encoder breaks ties. In one eight-symbol example, favoring shorter subtrees reduced the longest codeword from six bits to four. Both versions still averaged 2.571 bits per symbol.

Matrix chain.title: When the cheapest matrix multiplication costs more overall
Matrix chain.summary: Take 1 tried different ways to group four matrices being multiplied together. For its strongest example, choosing the cheapest adjacent pair each time took 952 multiplications of individual numbers. Planning the full order cut that to 338.

Coprime pairs.title: Counting pairs that share no factor greater than one
Coprime pairs.summary: Take 1 counted ordered pairs drawn from 1 through 100 million by grouping them by greatest common divisor. About 60.793% of the ten quadrillion pairs were coprime, close to the large-range prediction of six divided by pi squared.

Uniform draw.title: Reusing random bits when a draw gets rejected
Uniform draw.summary: Take 1 compared two ways to draw uniformly from 129 outcomes using fair coin flips. Starting over after each rejection took 15.88 flips on average. Recycling the leftover possibilities cut that to 8.95 flips and kept each outcome equally likely in the exhaustive checks.
